The viola caipira is a Brazilian ten-string guitar, its strings in five paired courses, and a chordophone descended from the Portuguese viola and traceable to the Latin guitar and the lute family. It is usually played in open tunings, plucked with the fingers of the right hand rather than a pick, close to classical and flamenco technique. It is common in caipira music and in subgenres such as the moda de viola, the caipira pagode and the catira, and it appears in northeastern and folk music too; early on the Jesuits used it in catechising indigenous people, and it entertained settlers and herders.
卡伊皮拉維奧拉源自葡萄牙維奧拉，譜系可上溯拉丁吉他與阿拉伯-波斯魯特系樂器。葡萄: The viola caipira comes from the Portuguese viola, a lineage that goes back to the Latin guitar and to instruments of the Arab-Persian lute family. After the Portuguese viola reached Brazil it was used early on by the Jesuits in catechising indigenous people, and it entertained Portuguese-Brazilian settlers and herders. It was later made from good local woods, close to the ten-string Braga and Amarante violas of northern Portugal. It became the basis of caipira music and of folk subgenres such as the moda de viola, the caipira pagode and the catira, and it once played urban music such as choro, samba and maxixe before being largely replaced there by the acoustic guitar. In 2004 a national association of viola players was founded, and the Ministry of Culture made the preservation of the viola tradition a matter of national interest.

The soundboard is mostly spruce or pine, and the back and sides use harder woods to strengthen the resonance. The neck and the pegbox use hard, durable wood. The strings are usually nylon or gut, in five double courses. The bridge and the nut are of bone or an ivory substitute, and some parts use metal fittings to stiffen the structure.
卡伊皮拉維奧拉音色明亮而溫暖，具有獨特的鼻音共鳴質感。其音域為中高音區，音色相較: The viola caipira has a bright, warm timbre with a distinctive nasal resonance. Its range is the middle and upper register, and it carries further than a classical guitar, with a clearly folk character. The sound the strings make through the soundbox has a touch of metal to it, giving a plain but expressive result. What sets it apart is that it combines the softness of the classical guitar with the brightness of the folk guitar while keeping the local colour of Brazilian folk music. The low register is warm and round, the high clear and bright, and the resonance lasts well. This character makes it easy to recognise in Brazilian folk music and lets it set the mood of rural and traditional music.
